# THREAD B — Mentorship / unblocking / the multiplier effect

## B1. Andy Grove — the origin of "your output includes your effect on others"
Andrew S. Grove, *High Output Management* (1983; Vintage reissue 1995).

The line, stated in the book's introduction — note the **"or influence"** clause, which is what extends it past managers to ICs:

> "**The output of a manager is the output of the organizational units under his or her supervision or influence.**"
> — Andy Grove, *High Output Management*, Introduction. Quoted verbatim at https://tylerdevries.com/book-summaries/high-output-management/ and https://www.becausetech.rocks/blog/high-output-management/ ("The book itself states the key take-away conveniently already in the introduction in a very clear way"). Book page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Output_Management

The leverage formalism that follows from it:

> "**A manager's output is thus the sum of the result of individual activities having varying degrees of leverage.**"
> "The extent to which that output is thereby increased is determined by the leverage of that activity—L1, L2, and so on."
> "**Clearly the key to high output means being sensitive to the leverage of what you do during the day.**"
> "**The art of management lies in the capacity to select from the many activities of seemingly comparable significance the one or two or three that provide leverage well beyond the others and concentrate on them.**"
> — Grove, *High Output Management*, quoted at https://www.thrivestreetadvisors.com/leadership-library/high-output-management

And the one most directly about mentoring:

> "**Training is one of the highest-leverage activities a manager can perform.**"
> — Grove, *High Output Management*, quoted at https://tylerdevries.com/book-summaries/high-output-management/

Contemporary corroboration that the "or influence" reading was intended broadly — the *Washington Post*'s 1983 review, quoted on the book's Wikipedia page, called it an "interesting, down-to-earth book that is **useful to anyone who influences the work of others, directly or indirectly.**" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Output_Management)

## B5. SPACE — the explicit refutation of single-dimension and individual-only productivity
Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Butler, Houck, *ACM Queue* 2021. URL: https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124

Framing:

> "**Far too often teams or managers attempt to measure developer productivity with simple metrics, attempting to capture it all with 'one metric that matters.'**"

> "**The most important takeaway from exposing these myths is that productivity cannot be reduced to a single dimension (or metric!).** The prevalence of these myths and the need to bust them motivated our work to develop a practical multidimensional framework, because **only by examining a constellation of metrics in tension can we understand and influence developer productivity.**"

**Myth: Productivity is all about developer activity**

> "This is one of the most common myths, and it can cause undesirable outcomes and developer dissatisfaction. Sometimes, higher volumes of activity appear for various reasons: working longer hours may signal developers having to 'brute-force' work to overcome bad systems or poor planning… On the other hand, **increased activity may reflect better engineering systems… or better collaboration and communication with team members in unblocking their changes and code reviews.**"

> "**Activity metrics alone do not reveal which of these is the case, so they should never be used in isolation either to reward or to penalize developers. Even straightforward metrics such as number of pull requests, commits, or code reviews are prone to errors because of gaps in data and measurement errors**, and systems that report these metrics will miss the benefits of collaboration seen in peer programming or brainstorming."

**Myth: Productivity is only about individual performance** — this is the one you want in full:

> "**While individual performance is important, contributing to the success of the team is also critical to measuring productivity. Measures of performance that balance the developer, team, and organization are important. Similar to team sports, success is judged both by a player's personal performance as well as the success of their team. A developer who optimizes only for their own personal productivity may hurt the productivity of the team. More team-focused activities such as code reviews, on-call rotations, and developing and managing engineering systems help maintain the quality of the code base and the product/service. Finding the right balance in optimizing for individual, team, and organizational productivity, as well as understanding possible tradeoffs, is key.**"

**Myth: One productivity metric can tell us everything**

> "One common myth about developer productivity is that it produces a universal metric, and that this 'one metric that matters' can be used to score teams on their overall work and to compare teams across an organization and even an industry. **This isn't true. Productivity represents several important dimensions of work and is greatly influenced by the context in which the work is done.**"

**Myth: Productivity measures are useful only for managers**

> "Developers often say that productivity measures aren't useful. This may come from the misuse of measures by leaders or managers… **but it's important to note that developers have found value in tracking their own productivity—both for personal reasons and for communicating with others.**"

**Myth: Productivity is only about engineering systems and developer tools** — the invisible-work myth, and the strongest single line in the paper for Thread B:

> "**Often the critical work needed to keep the environment and culture healthy can be 'invisible' to many members of the organization or to metrics traditionally used for measuring productivity. Work such as morale building, mentoring, and knowledge sharing are all critical to supporting a productive work environment and yet are often not measured. The 'invisible' work that benefits the overall productivity of the team is just as important as other more commonly-measured dimensions.**"

On the **Collaboration and communication** dimension specifically — the individual-cost / team-benefit tradeoff, named outright:

> "**Work that contributes to a team's outcomes or supports another team member's productivity may come at the expense of an individual's productivity and their own ability to get into a state of flow, potentially reducing motivation and satisfaction.** Effective collaboration, however, can drive down the need for some individual activities (e.g., unnecessary code reviews and rework), improve system performance (**faster pull request merges may improve quality by avoiding bugs**), and help sustain productivity and avoid… burnout."

> "Understanding and measuring team productivity and team member expectations are, however, complicated because of items that are difficult to measure such as **invisible work** and articulation work for coordinating and planning team tasks."

And on how the definition of productivity changes behavior:

> "**For example, a team where 'productivity = lines of code' alone is very different from a team where 'productivity = lines of code AND code review quality AND customer satisfaction.'** In this case, you have kept a (problematic, but probably embedded) metric about productivity and output, but **nudged perceptions about productivity in a direction that also values both teamwork (by valuing thoughtful code reviews) and the end user.**"

The paper's own conclusion: "**Developer productivity is about more than an individual's activity levels or the efficiency of the engineering systems relied on to ship software, and it cannot be measured by a single metric or dimension.**"

The SPACE sidebar on incident management repeats the pattern with an explicitly named list of the multiplier activities: "**More team-focused activities such as knowledge sharing, preparing troubleshooting guides to aid other team members, mentoring juniors and new members of the team, doing proper handoffs and assignment/re-assignments are important aspects.**"

## B6. Google Project Aristotle — individual performance did NOT predict team effectiveness
Google re:Work, "Guide: Understand team effectiveness" (Project Aristotle).
URL: https://rework.withgoogle.com/en/guides/understanding-team-effectiveness (re:Work has been retired; archived copy of the print guide: https://web.archive.org/web/2021/https://rework.withgoogle.com/print/guides/5721312655835136/)

Method: "Using over 35 different statistical models on hundreds of variables"; teams "ranged from three to fifty individuals (with a median of nine members)."

The headline:

> "**The researchers found that what really mattered was less about who is on the team, and more about how the team worked together.**"

The five dynamics, in order of importance: **psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, impact.**

> "Of the five key dynamics of effective teams that the researchers identified, **psychological safety was by far the most important.** The Google researchers found that individuals on teams with higher psychological safety are less likely to leave Google, they're more likely to harness the power of diverse ideas from their teammates, they bring in more revenue, and **they're rated as effective twice as often by executives.**"

**The kill-shot for "just measure individual output":**

> "The researchers also discovered which variables were **not** significantly connected with team effectiveness at Google: Colocation of teammates (sitting together in the same office) · Consensus-driven decision making · Extroversion of team members · **Individual performance of team members** · Workload size · Seniority · Team size · Tenure"

Also relevant: "Executives were most concerned with results (e.g., sales numbers or product launches), but **team members said that team culture was the most important measure of team effectiveness.**"

## Two things to flag before you build an argument on this

**1. The strongest counter-citation to "measure review turnaround per engineer" comes from the same people you'd cite for it.** SPACE says code-review velocity "is both an individual- and a team-level metric" — that supports you. But DX Core 4 (Noda/Tacho, Dec 2024) says of its Speed metric: "**It is critical that this metric is never used at the individual level or tied to performance evaluations.**" And SPACE itself says activity metrics "**should never be used in isolation either to reward or to penalize developers.**" The defensible position is *review turnaround as a visible, attributable signal used for coordination and self-management* — not as a performance-review score.

**2. Google's one-business-day rule has a stated exception that cuts against pure latency optimization**: "**If you are in the middle of a focused task, such as writing code, don't interrupt yourself to do a code review.**" Google's own resolution is to optimize *response* latency at natural break points, not to make reviewers interrupt-driven. DevEx makes the same point from the other side: "seemingly fast code review turnaround times may still feel disruptive to developers if code reviews regularly interrupt their work progress."
